name: Roman urine tooth whitening

card.summary: An ancient Roman dental-cosmetic practice in which urine, sometimes mixed with other ingredients, was used to make teeth look whiter.
card.note: Historical practice; urine is not a recognised modern whitening agent and modern whitening uses peroxide products.

quick.overview:
Roman dentists and their clients are reported to have used urine to whiten teeth, in a culture where bright teeth signalled beauty and wealth. The goal was the same as today's whitening: a lighter, cleaner-looking smile.

Accounts describe urine used alone or mixed with goat milk. Urine breaks down into ammonia over time, and Romans also used stale urine for washing cloth. No modern trial has tested the practice, and today's whitening relies on peroxide-based products.
quick.how: Historical accounts describe a rinse or rub applied to the teeth, sometimes with urine blended with goat milk. Details of frequency and results are not documented in the sources consulted, and the practice is not described here as a method to follow.
quick.risks: Urine is a body waste product that can carry bacteria, and modern dentistry does not use it. Ammonia is an irritant. Professional whitening today uses hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide under established protocols.

lead: Roman urine tooth whitening refers to the reported use in ancient Rome of urine, sometimes mixed with goat milk, to brighten the teeth.[1][2] White teeth were prized by the Romans as a sign of beauty and wealth, and false teeth made of bone, ivory and paste were also popular.[3]

People in that period used the practice for the same appearance goal as modern whitening: lighter teeth and a brighter smile. Urine was also a familiar everyday material, since fermented urine was used in antiquity for washing clothing and in cloth and hide processing, and the emperors Nero and Vespasian taxed the urine trade.[1]
No clinical study has tested urine as a whitener. Modern whitening works by peroxide compounds releasing free radicals that break down pigment molecules in the tooth.[2]

chain: Urine (or urine and goat milk) applied to the teeth
Used to remove staining as Romans understood it
angle.text: Romans reportedly used urine as a tooth cleaner and whitener because bright teeth were a mark of beauty and status. It is documented as a historical aesthetic habit rather than a tested technique.

infobox: Urine, sometimes mixed with goat milk[2]

paras: Wikipedia's article on tooth whitening reports that Roman dentists used urine mixed with goat milk to whiten teeth, and notes that pearly white teeth symbolised beauty and wealth.[2] The article on urine states more briefly that urine was used for whitening teeth in Ancient Rome, citing a dentistry textbook.[1]

Romans valued white teeth, and false teeth from bone, ivory and paste were popular items; oral hygiene was far below modern standards.[3] Fermented urine was in wider use across antiquity to wash fabric, remove hair from hides, act as a dye mordant and clean rust, and the emperors Nero and Vespasian taxed the urine trade.[1] Urea in urine breaks down to ammonia, which helps explain its cleaning role.[1]

Later European methods included filing teeth and applying acid in the late 17th century, an approach that eroded enamel.[2] Oxalic acid was proposed from 1877, followed by calcium hypochlorite, and custom-tray peroxide bleaching was introduced in the late 1960s by orthodontist William Klusmeier.[2] Carbamide peroxide releases hydrogen peroxide, which breaks pigment molecules into smaller, less coloured fragments.[2]
No studies found. Studies of peroxide whitening exist but concern a different method.
